title: Family
description: Name your relatives, introduce them and answer the questions everyone will ask about your family.

guide.title: Older or younger? Kannada always says
guide.text:
Kannada has no plain word for 'brother' or 'sister'. You must say whether the person is older or younger than you:

ಅಣ್ಣ (anna) elder brother; ತಮ್ಮ (tamma) younger brother; ಅಕ್ಕ (akka) elder sister; ತಂಗಿ (tangi) younger sister.

Parents and grandparents: ಅಪ್ಪ (appa) father; ಅಮ್ಮ (amma) mother; ತಾತ (taata) or ಅಜ್ಜ (ajja) grandfather; ಅಜ್ಜಿ (ajji) grandmother. The formal words ತಂದೆ (tande) father and ತಾಯಿ (taayi) mother are used in writing and on forms.

Marriage and children: ಗಂಡ (ganda) husband; ಹೆಂಡತಿ (hendati) wife; ಮಗ (maga) son; ಮಗಳು (magalu) daughter; ಮಗು (magu) child, baby; ಮಕ್ಕಳು (makkalu) children.

Uncles and aunts depend on the side of the family and on age. Father's elder brother is ದೊಡ್ಡಪ್ಪ (doddappa, 'big father'), his younger brother ಚಿಕ್ಕಪ್ಪ (chikkappa, 'small father'); mother's elder sister is ದೊಡ್ಡಮ್ಮ (doddamma), her younger sister ಚಿಕ್ಕಮ್ಮ (chikkamma). Mother's brother is ಮಾವ (maava) and father's sister is ಅತ್ತೆ (atte) - these two words also mean father-in-law and mother-in-law.

guide.title: Respect inside the family
guide.text:
Elders are spoken about with avaru / ivaru and a plural verb, even your own parents: ivaru nanna amma, 'this is my mother'; appa bartaare, 'Father is coming'; nanna taata halliyalli iddaare, 'my grandfather is in the village'.

Younger relatives take the singular: nanna tamma kaalejige hogtaane; nanna tangi odtiddaale.

For an elder brother or sister both are heard; the plural is the safer, more polite choice.

Husband and wife: introducing a spouse to others, people use the respectful ivaru.

The same family words are used to address strangers politely: anna or akka to someone a little older than you, amma to an older woman, taata or ajji to the elderly.

examples.english: My grandfather lives in the village.
My younger brother goes to college.

guide.title: Talking about your family
guide.text:
'I have a brother' uses the dative pattern: nanage + relative + form of iru. Count people with the human number words: obba anna (one elder brother), obbalu tangi (one younger sister), ibbaru makkalu (two children), mooru jana (three people).

'Family' in the sense of household is usually expressed with ಮನೆ (mane), 'house': nimma maneyalli eshtu jana iddaare? 'how many people are there in your house?'. The formal word is ಕುಟುಂಬ (kutumba).

Marriage 'happens to you': ಮದುವೆ ಆಗಿದೆ (maduve aagide) 'is married', literally 'marriage has happened'; ಮದುವೆ ಆಗಿಲ್ಲ (maduve aagilla) 'is not married'. These are everyday questions in India and are not considered intrusive.

phrases.note: ivaru is the respectful word for 'this person'.
Younger brother: tamma (ತಮ್ಮ). anna here has the retroflex ಣ್ಣ.
For counting people use 'ibbaru' (two persons), not 'eradu'.

phrases.english: How many people are there in your family?
phrases.note: Literally 'in your house' - the usual way to ask about family.

phrases.english: My grandfather lives in the village.
phrases.note: 'taata' is usual around Bengaluru; elsewhere in Karnataka you will hear 'ajja' (ಅಜ್ಜ).
ellaroo = everyone. A polite question after greeting someone.
For 'husband': ivaru nanna ganda (ಇವರು ನನ್ನ ಗಂಡ).

phrases.english: My elder sister lives in Mysuru.
phrases.note: Plural verb out of respect for an elder.

phrases.english: My younger brother goes to college.

phrases.native: ನಮ್ಮ ಅಜ್ಜಿ ತುಂಬಾ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಅಡುಗೆ ಮಾಡ್ತಾರೆ.
phrases.roman: namma ajji tumbaa chennaagi aduge maadtaare.
phrases.literal: our grandmother very well cooking does
phrases.note: namma ('our') is the natural word for one's own family members.
